system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 26 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with end-stage renal disease, diabetes, morbid obesity, and a history of recurrent abscesses and thromboses was admitted for a right groin abscess that had drained spontaneously. She was febrile on presentation and received incision and drainage in the ED, followed by IV vancomycin. Blood cultures remained negative, and she remained afebrile throughout the hospitalization. A CT scan showed no deep pelvic infection, and a right lower extremity ultrasound ruled out DVT despite initial concern on imaging. The abscess improved with packing and antibiotics. Her INR remained therapeutic on warfarin, and she continued her home medications for heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, and diabetes. She completed a dialysis session on the day of discharge and was transitioned to oral sevelamer and Nephrocaps. She was discharged to extended care with wound care instructions, a seven-day course of vancomycin via dialysis, and guidance to monitor weight and symptoms.
problems: Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

vomiting in addition to persistently bleeding right groin abscess.  The
patient is on hemodialysis and can get intravenous contrast.

COMPARISON:  CT pelvis with contrast, ___.  CT abdomen and pelvis,
___ and a DVT study ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Multidetector CT imaging of the abdomen and pelvis were obtained
after the administration of 130 cc of Omnipaque intravenous contrast. 
Sagittal and coronal reformats were generated and reviewed.

FINDINGS:  The imaged lung bases demonstrate mild dependent atelectasis.  No
pleural or pericardial effusion is seen.  Mild coronary arterial, mitral and
aortic annular calcifications are seen.

The liver enhances homogeneously, without focal lesions.  There is no intra-
or extra-hepatic biliary dilatation.  Minimal pneumobilia is seen in the left
hepatic lobe, which is secondary to prior sphincterotomy.  There is stable
mild dilation of the CBD measuring 13mm. No intraductal filling defects or
masses are seen. The gallbladder, adrenal glands, spleen, and pancreas are
normal.  The native kidneys are atrophic with multiple subcentimeter
hypodensities, likely cysts, indicative of chronic medical renal disease.   A
left common femoral approach venous dialysis catheter ends in the hepatic IVC.
Moderate amount of fecal load is seen throughout the entire colon.  Note of
diverticulosis in the cecum is made.  The stomach and small bowel loops are
normal.  There is no evidence of bowel obstruction or ischemia on this single
phase study.  The abdominal aorta and iliac arteries have moderate
atherosclerotic calcification without aneurysmal dilation.  Extensive
atherosclerotic calcification is seen at the origin of the SMA, causing
stenosis of the same.  There is no intra-abdominal free fluid or air.  No
significant retroperitoneal or mesenteric lymphadenopathy is seen.

CT OF THE PELVIS WITH INTRAVENOUS CONTRAST:  The uterus is enlarged, with
multiple calcified masses, consistent with fibroids.  The urinary bladder is
normal.  The rectum is impacted with stool.  No significant pelvic
lymphadenopathy or free fluid is seen.  Again seen is subtle asymmetric
hypoattenuation within the right common femoral vein as before, which could be
secondary to mixing artifact or a DVT.

BONES AND SOFT TISSUES:  No bone lesions suspicious for infection or
malignancy are detected.  No abnormality is identified in the subcutaneous
tissues of the right inguinal region in the imaged portion.

IMPRESSION:
1.  No acute intra-abdominal or pelvic pathology.
2.  Possible filling defect in the right common femoral vein, which could
indicate deep venous thrombosis.
3.  Stable mild dilation of common bile duct measuring up to 13 mm. No
intraductal filling defects or masses are seen via CT, although MRCP/ERCP is
more sensitive.

INDICATION:  ___ female with reported vascular anomaly and right groin
abscess instrumentation one week ago with subsequent bleeding.

COMPARISON:  CT dated ___ and ___.

Recent prior surgical debridement:  ___.

FINDINGS:  Targeted sonogram was performed over a packed wound along the
inferolateral aspect of the abdominal pannus on the right, demonstrating a 1.4
x 1.2 x 1 cm saccular structure with internal bidirectional vascular flow,
consistent with a pseudoaneurysm.  Inferior to this is a 1.7 x 0.8 cm anechoic
nonvascular region which could represent residual collection.  More laterally
in the right groin, the femoral artery and vein appear patent, with normal
arterial and venous waveforms.

IMPRESSION:
1.  1.4 x 1.2 cm right lower abdominal wall pseudoaneurysm subjacent to the
packed wound, superficial in location, likely arising from a small epigastric
arterial branch.

2.  Likely persistent fluid collection caudal to the pseudoaneurysm measuring
at least 1.7 x 0.8 cm.

3.  Patent and unremarkable femoral vessels.

Findings reported to Dr. ___ via phone at 2:15 p.m. on ___.

CT DATED ___

INDICATION:  ? AV fistula, infected vessel or pseudoaneurysm per CTA runoff to
mid thigh.

COMPARISON:  Comparison is made to previous CTs, most recently dated ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Axial MDCT images acquired non-contrast and post-uneventful
Omnipaque administration through the lower pelvis to the mid thigh.  Coronal
and sagittal reformats were obtained.

FINDINGS:

CT PELVIS:  There are multiple calcified fibroids within the uterus, the
largest measuring 4.5 x 3.3 cm within the right side of the uterus (2:31)  The
urinary bladder is normal in appearance.  The rectum and sigmoid are normal in
appearance.  The visualized small and large bowel are normal.  There is no
pelvic adenopathy.  There is no free fluid or free air.
No suspicious osseous sclerotic or lucent lesions identified.

CTA:  There is moderate calcification of the distal aorta, common iliac
arteries, superficial femoral artery and profunda femoris arteries
bilaterally.  There is a hemodialysis catheter within the left common femoral
vein extending to the distal IVC.  The common iliac arteries, superficial
femoral arteries and profunda femoris arteries are patent bilaterally.  There
is retrograde filling of the common femoral veins bilaterally . AV fistula
noted (3:88). Thrombus present within both common femoral veins which are
expanded. The left SFV is atrectic. There are multiple collaterals noted
within the right inguinal region.

There is a discrete well-rounded density adjacent to the skin defect within
the right labia, which enhances post-contrast (3:105).  There is subcutaneous
edema within the subcutaneous tissues bilaterally.  Bilateral subcentimeter
inguinal lymph nodes.  No pathologically enlarged lymph nodes.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Bilateral common femoral DVT's. Atretic left SFA indicating prior
thrombosis.
2.  Right AV fistula.  No evidence of pseudoaneurysm.
3.  Fibroid uterus.
4.  New discrete enhancing rounded hyperdensity within the right labia
adjacent to the skin defect site.  This could represent a small hematoma or
lesion.  Clinical correlation is recommended.

WET READ by ___ on ___ 11:13 ___
Findings of #1,#2 and #3 were discussed by phone with Dr. ___.

TYPE OF EXAMINATION:  Chest AP portable single view.

INDICATION:  ___ female patient status post groin arterial venous
fistula resection with high blood loss, evaluate for CHF or effusion.

FINDINGS:  AP single view of the chest has been obtained with patient in
supine position.  Comparison is made with a previous similar examination of
___, which also was performed with the patient in supine position. 
Moderate cardiac enlargement as before.  Heart size may have increased
slightly.  However, portable technique in supine position does not allow
precise assessment.  Comparison with the next previous study clearly
identifies a new parenchymal density in the left hemithorax in perihilar
position extending into the left upper lobe.  The previously identified left
lower lobe linear densities suspicious for atelectasis persist.  No new
pulmonary abnormalities in the right hemithorax and no pneumothorax identified
on either side.  The patient is intubated and the ETT terminates in the
trachea some 5 cm above the level of the carina.

IMPRESSION:  New parenchymal infiltrates in mid and left upper lung field.  As
patient apparently was in supine position during the last ten days, consider
possibility of aspiration pneumonitis in this unusual location.

INDICATION:  History of bilateral upper extremity failed AV fistulas and
bilateral internal jugular thromboses.  Poor intravenous access, in need of
PICC.

Technique:  Ultrasound and fluoroscopic-guided PICC placement.

PROCEDURE:  Written informed consent was obtained prior to the procedure,
explaining the risks, benefits and alternatives.  The patient was laid supine
on the angiographic table.  A preprocedure timeout was performed using three
patient identifiers and confirming the procedure to be performed.

A site suitable for PICC placement in the right upper extremity was selected
and using sterile technique and under local anesthesia, the right basilic vein
was punctured under direct ultrasound guidance using a micropuncture set. 
Hard copies of ultrasound images were obtained before and immediately after
establishing intravenous access.  A peel-away sheath was then placed over a
guidewire and a single-lumen PICC measuring 38 cm in length was placed through
the peel-away sheath with tip positioned in the distal SVC under fluoroscopic
guidance.  Position of the catheter was confirmed by a fluoroscopic spot film.

The peel-away sheath and guidewire were removed.  The catheter was secured to
the skin, flushed, and a sterile dressing applied.

The patient tolerated the procedure well.  There were no immediate
complications.

The attending physician, ___, was present and supervising throughout the
procedure.

IMPRESSION:  Uncomplicated ultrasound and fluoroscopically-guided single-lumen
PICC via the right basilic vein.  Final internal length is 38 cm with tip in
the distal SVC.  The line is ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you came in because your groin wound started bleeding during dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it just started oozing. I was scared. My blood pressure dropped, they said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. Your hematocrit dropped from 36 to 30, and your INR was high at 3.0. We stopped the bleeding with medication and packing. But we need to find out why this keeps happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it infection again? I just had that abscess drained last week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking into that. A scan showed a possible pseudoaneurysm near your wound, but a later CT confirmed something more serious—an arteriovenous fistula in your groin. That means an artery and vein are connected abnormally, which can cause bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Can that be fixed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it will require surgery. We’ll need to go in and close off those abnormal connections. Given your history—ESRD, diabetes, clotting issues—it’s high risk, but necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m already on warfarin. Isn’t that making it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It contributes. Your INR was 3.0, which is high. We’ve held your warfarin for now. We’ll restart it later when it’s safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your regular schedule. We’ll coordinate it around your care. For now, you’re admitted for monitoring and prep for surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable. The CT confirmed the AV fistula comes from the profunda and common femoral arteries. We’ve scheduled surgery for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I lose a lot of blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There is risk, yes. These vessels are large. We’re preparing for possible transfusion. But the team is experienced, and we’ll do everything to keep you safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re in recovery. The surgery went well. We took down the fistulas. But you did lose about 4.5 liters of blood. You received fluids, red cells, and FFP. You’re in the ICU for close monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So much blood… am I going to be okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re stable now. Hemodynamically okay. We’re watching your kidney function and heart closely. You’ll move to the floor tomorrow if all stays well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re off the ventilator and moving to the regular floor today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My wound still hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It will for a while. We’re keeping it clean and watching for infection. You’re still on antibiotics from before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We need to talk. On day 6 after surgery, you developed redness and drainage at the incision site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it infected again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We opened and packed the wound. The culture grew two bacteria: Klebsiella and Proteus. They’re resistant to many antibiotics, but sensitive to meropenem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you’re changing my antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re switching from vancomycin, cipro, and flagyl to IV meropenem. It covers both organisms effectively.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need it long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for about two weeks. We’ll give it through a PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re placing a PICC line today for your antibiotics. You have poor vein access, so we’ll use ultrasound and X-ray guidance in your right arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get local anesthesia. It’s a quick procedure. The line will stay in for your antibiotics and then be removed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC was placed successfully yesterday. Your wound is being debrided daily. We’re seeing granulation tissue, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s granulation tissue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s new tissue that forms during healing. Pink and bumpy. It means your wound is starting to close from the inside.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need the infection under control and the wound stable. You’ll likely go to extended care for wound management and IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting a wound VAC today. It’s a vacuum device that helps pull fluid out and encourages healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it be uncomfortable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some people feel a pulling sensation, but it’s usually well tolerated. We’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your wound is improving. Less drainage, more granulation. The VAC is working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood sugars? They’ve been high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, stress and steroids can raise them. We’ve adjusted your insulin. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest wound culture confirmed Klebsiella and Proteus. Both are sensitive to meropenem, so we’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are they dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They can be, especially with your health conditions. But meropenem is strong and effective. We’re confident it will clear the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. The wound no longer needs debridement. We’ll keep the VAC a few more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I start walking more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with assistance. We’ll get physical therapy to help you build strength. But avoid straining the groin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your dialysis went well yesterday. Your labs are stable. We’re planning for discharge in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Where will I go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To extended care. You’ll continue the VAC, get IV meropenem through the PICC, and have wound checks daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing discharge. You’ll go with the VAC, PICC line, and a 14-day course of meropenem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most are resuming: simvastatin, pantoprazole, sevelamer, and warfarin at a lower dose. Paroxetine is cut in half. We’re adding cinacalcet for your calcium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your surgeon in two weeks. The wound team will manage the VAC and PICC. Call us if you develop fever, increased redness, or bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—the CT also showed fibroids and a small spot in your labia. It could be a hematoma. Your gynecologist will evaluate it later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. It’s small. We’ll follow up after you’ve healed from this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Hemodynamically stable, eating well, wound improving. We’re scheduling discharge for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was so scared when I started bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. But you’ve been strong. This was complex, but we’ve addressed the fistula and infection. Now it’s about healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last check. Your wound is ready for transfer. Remember: keep the VAC on, watch for fever, and don’t skip dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team is here. You’re being discharged to extended care with wound VAC and PICC for antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay strong. Call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good luck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a smooth recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope so.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve come a long way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks to you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with end-stage renal disease, diabetes, morbid obesity, and a history of recurrent infections and thromboses was admitted after spontaneous bleeding from a recent right groin abscess during dialysis. She was found to have an arteriovenous fistula involving the right common femoral and profunda arteries, requiring surgical repair with significant blood loss. Postoperatively, she developed a wound infection with Klebsiella pneumoniae and Proteus mirabilis, necessitating a change to IV meropenem. A wound VAC was placed, and a PICC line was inserted for antibiotic administration. She remained hemodynamically stable, resumed dialysis, and was transitioned to extended care with a plan for continued wound management, IV antibiotics, and follow-up. Her warfarin was restarted, and medications were adjusted for her comorbidities.
